q: According to the OEG, what are the three major causes of fatalities in engine-out emergencies?
a: Loss of directional control, climb performance, and flying airspeed
d: Feathering the wrong engine, fuel exhaustion, and structural overload
Loss of directional control, engine fire, and failure to feather
Gear left down, flaps left down, and windmilling propeller drag
why: Engine-out accidents usually come down to losing control (Vmc), losing the ability to climb, or letting airspeed decay into a stall, alone or in combination. The other choices are specific errors that lead to those outcomes.

q: When is an engine failure during takeoff considered most critical?
a: The 2–3 seconds right after liftoff, while accelerating to climb speed
d: The first 2–3 seconds of the takeoff roll, while the airplane is well below Vmc
The moment of rotation, as the nosewheel leaves the runway
Just after gear retraction, while passing about 400 feet AGL at Vyse
why: Right after liftoff the airplane is slow, low and still accelerating toward climb speed. It may be controllable, but its one-engine climb performance is far below optimum, so it may not be able to keep flying.

q: Most light twins are controllable just above Vmc. Why is an engine failure right after liftoff still so dangerous?
a: Performance is so poor that continued flight may be impossible
d: The airplane is below Vso and will stall almost immediately
The rudder has no authority until the gear is retracted
The propeller cannot be feathered until the airplane reaches Vyse
why: Being able to control the airplane does not mean it can climb. Close to Vmc and still accelerating, it is far from its best single-engine climb condition.

q: To reduce the risk of an engine failure on takeoff, what should your pre-takeoff briefing (or self-briefing) cover?
a: Your plan of action if an engine fails during takeoff or climb
d: The planned cruise altitude, power setting, and expected fuel burn
Passenger seat belts, emergency exits, and the no-smoking rule
The departure frequency, transponder code, and first navigation fix
why: The OEG's first mitigation is a briefing that commits the PIC to a plan for an engine failure or other emergency at any point in the takeoff and initial climb. That way the response isn't being invented under stress.

q: Which performance figures does the OEG say you should know before a multi-engine takeoff?
a: Accelerate-stop/go distances, single-engine service ceiling, OEI climb rate
d: Cruise true airspeed, fuel flow at 65% power, and maximum range
Landing distance, maximum demonstrated crosswind, and maneuvering speed
Two-engine service ceiling, never-exceed speed, and best glide speed
why: These numbers, along with terrain and obstacles in the flight path, tell you whether you can stop or continue if an engine fails. The OEG adds that you should allow generous margins for real-world performance.

q: You are departing a short runway at a high density altitude airport. Which preparation best supports a fast decision if an engine fails?
a: Know runway length, accelerate-stop distance, and an obstacle-free path
d: Know the two-engine climb rate, planned cruise altitude, and cruise power
Know the nearest VOR frequency, the destination ATIS, and the squawk code
Know the best glide speed, maximum landing weight, and Vfe
why: The OEG says to know your options before takeoff: runway length, a direction of flight free of obstacles, and the stop and go distances. Two-engine and cruise figures tell you nothing about the engine-out case.

q: Are most light twins certificated under 14 CFR Part 23 required to hold altitude on one engine in the takeoff configuration?
a: No; many aren't required to in any configuration, even at sea level
d: Yes, they must hold altitude at sea level and maximum gross weight
Yes, they must hold altitude up to their single-engine service ceiling
Yes, but only with the gear retracted and the flaps at takeoff
why: Part 23 as most light twins were certificated does not require a light twin to maintain altitude in the takeoff configuration with an engine inoperative, and many need not do so in any configuration. Today's 23.2120(b)(1) requires new level 1–2 low-speed twins that don't meet single-engine crashworthiness standards to show a 1.5% gradient at 5,000 ft, but in cruise configuration. Never assume the second engine guarantees a climb.

q: What common belief about losing an engine in a light twin does the OEG call mistaken?
a: That it will still perform at least half as well on one engine
d: That the airplane will yaw toward the inoperative engine
That a windmilling propeller adds a significant amount of drag
That Vmc can vary depending on which engine has failed
why: Climb comes from power beyond what level flight needs, so losing half the power costs far more than half the climb. For performance (not control) in the takeoff or landing configuration, think of a light twin as a single whose power is split between two engines.

q: In the OEG's typical engine-failure checklist, which memory items come right after maintaining control and Vyse?
a: Mixtures rich, propellers high RPM, throttles full power
d: Identify, verify, and feather the failed engine
Fuel selector to crossfeed, boost pumps on, mags checked
Cowl flap closed, alternator off, mixture to cutoff
why: After control and airspeed, you push everything forward (mixtures, props, throttles) for maximum available power, as the Seneca POH 3-11 also does. Then you clean up drag and identify the engine. Crossfeed and mags are troubleshooting steps, and the last choice is securing.

q: Which sequence matches the OEG's typical engine-failure memory flow?
a: Control, power up, clean up, identify, verify, fix or feather
d: Control, identify, verify, feather, then power up and clean up
Identify, verify, control, clean up, feather, then power up
Control, clean up, feather, identify, verify, then power up
why: Control and Vyse come first, then maximum power (mixtures, props, throttles), then drag cleanup, then identify, verify with the throttle, and fix or feather. The OEG's generic table lists gear before flaps; the AFH's typical checklist (FAA-H-8083-3C fig 13-21) lists flaps then gear, noting some airplanes do gear first. Your school's Seneca memory items: blue line 105 MPH, mixtures, props and throttles forward, flaps up, gear up, fuel pumps on (the AFM, POH 3-11, says airspeed above 90 MPH).

q: Why does the memory flow set full power and clean up drag before you identify the failed engine?
a: To get the best performance with the least risk of losing control
d: Because full power makes the gauges reveal the failed engine
Because the propeller can only feather at full throttle
Because the gear must be up before the prop can feather
why: The steps before Fix or Feather are there to put the airplane in its most favorable performance condition, the one least likely to end in loss of control, while you work out which engine quit.

q: An engine quits at 600 ft AGL on climb-out. You've completed control, power up, clean up, identify, and verify. What now?
a: Feather it immediately; secure it as time allows
d: Run the restart checklist first, then decide whether to feather
Leave it windmilling so a restart will be easier later
Switch its fuel selector to crossfeed and wait to see
why: At low altitude the OEG's Fix-or-Feather choice is to feather the affected engine immediately, because a windmilling prop adds a lot of drag when you can least afford it. Troubleshooting belongs at higher altitude, when there is time.

q: An engine fails at 7,000 ft in cruise with plenty of terrain clearance. After control, power up, identify, and verify, what is appropriate?
a: If time allows, try to find and fix the problem before feathering
d: Feather it at once; troubleshooting is never done in flight in a twin
Descend to pattern altitude first, then begin any troubleshooting
Shut off both boost pumps and wait for it to recover
why: With altitude and time, the Fix-or-Feather step allows an attempt to fix the problem. If that fails, you run a diagnosis or securing checklist. Control remains the first priority throughout.

q: During a Vmc demonstration, the nose keeps yawing toward the dead engine despite full rudder. What should you do immediately?
a: Retard the operating engine's throttle while lowering the pitch attitude
d: Advance the operating engine's throttle while raising the pitch attitude
Feather the windmilling engine while holding full rudder
Hold full rudder and aileron, and raise the nose to slow down further
why: Reducing power on the operating engine removes the asymmetric thrust that is causing the yaw. Lowering the nose restores airspeed and reduces the angle of attack.

q: When recovering from a Vmc demonstration, what condition do you establish before setting symmetrical power?
a: Straight flight on the entry heading at Vsse or Vyse
d: A climbing turn toward the good engine at Vxse
Straight flight on the entry heading at Vmc
Level flight on any heading at stall warning speed
why: You recover to straight flight on the original heading at Vsse or Vyse. Per the AFH, you then increase power on the operating engine and show controlled flight before restoring symmetrical power. The recovery does not include adding power to the windmilling engine by itself.

q: When Vmc is at or below stall speed, or density altitude prevents a true demo, what technique allows a safe Vmc demonstration?
a: Limit rudder travel artificially to simulate maximum available rudder
d: Perform the demonstration at a higher density altitude instead
Feather the inoperative propeller to lower its windmilling drag
Extend the gear and flaps so the stall happens at a higher speed
why: Blocking the rudder makes directional control run out at a speed well above the stall. Higher density altitude and feathering both lower Vmc, which makes the problem worse.

q: When rudder travel is artificially limited to demonstrate Vmc, at about what speed should the demonstration be done?
a: About 20 knots above Vs
d: About 5 knots above Vs
At Vs, with the stall warning sounding
At Vso, in the landing configuration
why: Running out of (limited) rudder about 20 knots above the stall keeps the demo clear of a stall with asymmetric power, which could become a spin, while still showing the loss of directional control.

q: During a Vmc demo you notice the stall signs late, and the airplane begins to roll and yaw. What should you do?
a: Pull both throttles back, lower the nose, get above Vmc (ideally Vsse)
d: Add full power on the good engine and pull the nose up to hold altitude
Feather the windmilling engine, then raise the nose to slow down
Hold full rudder and aileron against the roll and wait to reach Vyse
why: If nothing is done, the asymmetric thrust overpowers the controls and the airplane can roll over, stall and spin. Taking the power off and reducing the angle of attack stops this. Once level above Vmc you can bring power back on the good engine.

q: Why does the OEG suggest reducing both throttles, not just the operating one, when recovering from a botched Vmc demo?
a: To avoid any confusion about which throttle to reduce
d: Because the windmilling engine adds yaw when at idle
Because both throttles must be closed in order to feather
To let the propellers slow to their start-lock speed
why: When roll and yaw are developing fast, pulling both throttles guarantees that the power causing the problem comes off. Once the airplane is stable, you reapply power on the good engine.

q: During the takeoff roll, below Vmc, the left engine fails. What does the OEG direct?
a: Reject the takeoff: close both throttles; use rudder and brakes
d: Continue: lift off and accelerate in ground effect to Vyse
Feather the left engine first, then continue the takeoff roll
Partially reduce the right throttle and continue the takeoff
why: Below Vmc on the ground, the only way to keep directional control is to close both throttles promptly and use rudder and brakes. Continuing is not an option.
drop_reason: duplicate of o1-068 (engine failure on the takeoff roll below Vmc: close both throttles, abort); also o8-052. o7-021 and o7-035 keep 3C-9/3C-19 detail

q: Per the OEG, why should a twin not become airborne before its airspeed reaches and exceeds Vmc?
a: If an engine failed, directional control would be impossible
d: The landing gear cannot be retracted until the airspeed passes Vmc
The stall warning system does not function below Vmc
The propellers cannot be feathered at speeds below Vmc
why: Below Vmc, full rudder can't hold heading against an engine failure, so the OEG wants Vmc or more at lift-off. The Seneca's 25° short-field technique (70 MPH) and your school's 75 MPH flaps-up rotation lift off below the 80 MPH Vmc; if an engine fails there, retard the operating engine's throttle and lower the nose at once (POH 6-7).

q: Why does the OEG advise against practicing stalls with one engine inoperative, actual or simulated?
a: Risk of a Vmc loss of control, and a lot of altitude to recover
d: The operating engine may overheat at a high angle of attack
The stall warning does not work with an engine out
A feathered propeller can unfeather itself in a stall
why: Stalling with asymmetric power invites a Vmc roll and possible spin, and the recovery can take a lot of altitude.

q: In a steep turn, the inboard (lower-wing) engine suddenly fails. What tendency should you expect?
a: The high-wing engine tends to roll the airplane further into the bank
d: The airplane tends to roll back out of the bank toward wings level on its own
The nose pitches up sharply while the bank becomes shallower
No rolling tendency develops; yaw and bank cancel each other
why: With the low engine dead, the operating engine on the high wing tends to add roll into the turn, which can grow into a Vmc encounter. If the high-wing engine fails instead, the low engine tends to roll the airplane back toward level.

q: What should be your first action if an engine loses power during a steep turn?
a: Reduce the bank and return to level flight
d: Increase back pressure to hold altitude
Steepen the bank toward the dead engine
Feather immediately while holding the bank
why: Stall and Vmc risk are higher in a steep turn, so roll level right away. If the airplane is rolling into the turn, the OEG adds that you can reduce power on the operating engine (or both) until you are level.

q: Your left engine suddenly quits in cruise. What is your first priority?
a: Maintain aircraft control and airspeed
d: Identify and feather the failed engine
Declare an emergency with ATC
Attempt an immediate engine restart
why: Every engine-out procedure starts with flying the airplane: control and airspeed come before identifying, feathering, troubleshooting or talking to ATC.

q: After a power loss, the airplane yaws left and your left foot is idle. Before feathering the left engine, how do you verify?
a: Retard the left throttle
d: Pull the left mixture to cutoff
Turn the left magnetos off
Compare the left and right MP gauges
why: Closing the suspected throttle can be undone: if it's the wrong engine, the yaw increases and you push the throttle back up. Cutting the mixture or mags on the wrong engine could leave you with no power, and gauges can mislead.

q: Verifying a suspected failed engine, you retard its throttle and immediately need a clear change in rudder to hold heading. What does that tell you?
a: That engine was still making power; don't feather it
d: That engine has definitely failed; feather it now
Both engines are losing power at the same time
Its propeller has already gone to feather on its own
why: Retarding the throttle of a truly dead engine changes nothing, so no control change is needed. If you suddenly need different rudder, that engine was still contributing power: put the throttle back and re-identify before feathering anything.

q: What does 'dead foot, dead engine' mean?
a: The foot not pressing rudder is on the failed engine's side
d: The foot pressing hardest is on the failed engine's side
Press the rudder on the failed side to stop the yaw
Take both feet off the rudders to feel the yaw
why: You press rudder on the good engine's side to stop the yaw toward the dead engine. The idle ('dead') foot is on the side of the failed engine.

q: After a loud bang and a sudden yaw on climb-out, you're holding firm right rudder and your left foot is idle. Which engine most likely failed?
a: The left engine
d: The right engine
Neither; rudder pressure alone can't show it
Both; it is a symmetrical power loss
why: The airplane yaws toward the dead engine, so you need rudder on the opposite side. Right rudder with an idle left foot means the left engine. Then verify by retarding the left throttle.

q: Why can engine gauges mislead you when identifying a failed engine?
a: A windmilling prop can show high RPM, and MP can read near normal
d: The failed engine's gauges always drop to zero immediately
Both engines' gauges share a single sensor, so they always read the same
Engine gauges are only accurate above about 5,000 feet density altitude
why: Depending on whether the failure is partial or complete, the dead engine's MP can read close to the good engine's, and a windmilling prop keeps RPM up. A dead engine can look alive, so identify it with control inputs.

q: The right engine fails. Which way will the airplane yaw, and which rudder do you apply?
a: Yaws right; apply left rudder immediately
d: Yaws left; apply right rudder immediately
Yaws right; apply right rudder immediately
Yaws left; apply left rudder immediately
why: The good left engine's thrust swings the nose toward the dead right engine, and left rudder stops that yaw.

q: An engine fails while you are in IMC. What should get priority in your scan?
a: The flight instruments, holding heading and airspeed
d: The engine gauges, to find out which engine has failed
The fuel gauges, to rule out fuel starvation
The GPS, to locate the nearest airport
why: You identify the engine the same way as in VMC, but in IMC you keep scanning the flight instruments to hold heading (mainly with rudder) and airspeed. Rudder pressure still tells you which engine quit.

q: Immediately after an engine fails in IMC, before you correct, which way does the turn coordinator ball move?
a: Toward the operative engine
d: Toward the inoperative engine
It stays centered
Back and forth, with no trend
why: The airplane yaws toward the dead engine and the ball swings the other way, toward the good engine. Rudder on the good-engine side stops the yaw.

q: An engine fails after takeoff. The airplane is under control and can climb, but trees ahead must be cleared. Which speed should you fly?
a: Vxse
d: Vyse
Vsse
Vmc
why: Vxse gives the most altitude gain over the shortest distance on one engine, which is what clearing an obstacle needs. Vyse gives the best rate of climb, not the best angle.

q: An engine fails just before liftoff and you close both throttles to reject. Per the OEG, what do you use to keep the airplane on the runway?
a: Rudder, nosewheel steering and brakes, aggressively if needed
d: Rudder alone, since braking would skid you toward the dead engine
Power on the good engine plus rudder to hold the centerline
Ailerons into the dead engine plus light, gentle braking
why: With both throttles closed, directional control comes from rudder, nosewheel steering and brakes, and the OEG warns they may need to be used hard. Adding power on one engine would bring back the very yaw you are fighting.

q: In a rejected takeoff after an engine failure, what is the primary objective?
a: Keep control of the airplane as it decelerates
d: Stop the airplane in the shortest possible distance
Exit the runway at the nearest taxiway
Secure the failed engine before the airplane stops
why: Aggressive rudder, steering and braking may be needed, but what matters is staying in control while you slow down; the shortest possible stop is secondary.

q: A twin's calculated Vmc is 70 knots. Per the ACS, a simulated engine failure on the takeoff roll should be given before what speed?
a: 35 knots
d: 50 knots
65 knots
70 knots
why: The ACS calls for a simulated failure on the takeoff roll before 50 percent of the calculated Vmc: half of 70 is 35 knots. In the Seneca (Vmc 80 mph CAS) that would be before 40 mph.
drop_reason: duplicate of o8-051 (Vmc 70 kt: simulate before 35 kt, same distractors); Seneca note moved to o8-051

q: Just after liftoff, with the gear still down and runway remaining, an engine fails. What should you do?
a: Close both throttles and land on the remaining runway or overrun
d: Raise the gear, feather the failed engine, and then climb out at Vyse
Feather first, then decide whether to land or continue
Stay in ground effect and accelerate to Vyse before climbing out
why: With the gear still down, keep straight, close both throttles, lower the nose to hold airspeed, and make a normal landing ahead. The chances of cleaning up, feathering and accelerating under control are minimal. The Seneca POH 3-12a agrees when adequate runway remains.

q: In a twin with a single engine-driven hydraulic pump, why does losing that engine on takeoff matter for the gear?
a: Raising the gear requires a windmilling engine or a hand pump
d: The gear still retracts normally using the other engine's pump
The gear can only be raised by using the emergency extension system
The gear raises electrically, so there is no effect
why: With the pump's engine dead, the only ways to raise the gear are to let that engine windmill or to use a hand pump. Neither is practical during a takeoff emergency, which is one more reason to land ahead. (The Seneca's gear pump is electric, POH 2-4, so this case doesn't apply to it.)

q: An engine fails just after liftoff with the gear up. At Vyse with full power on the good engine, you are still sinking. What should you do?
a: Land under control ahead, descending at Vyse if needed
d: Raise the nose to hold altitude, letting speed bleed off
Turn back toward the runway while holding your altitude
Slow to Vxse to stop the descent and hold altitude
why: Near or above the single-engine ceiling you must land on essentially whatever lies ahead, or keep going ahead in a descent at Vyse. Trying to hold altitude by bleeding off airspeed is almost always fatal.

q: Per the OEG, what is almost invariably fatal after an engine failure on takeoff?
a: Staying airborne by bleeding off airspeed to hold altitude
d: Landing straight ahead in an off-airport field
Descending straight ahead at Vyse with the good engine at full power
Landing with the landing gear still retracted
why: The killer is insisting on flight the airplane can't sustain. A controlled landing, even off-airport or gear up, is far more survivable than a stall or Vmc roll.

q: After an engine failure on takeoff with the gear up and adequate climb performance, what are the four areas of concern, in order?
a: Control, configuration, climb, checklist
d: Aviate, navigate, communicate, checklist
Identify, verify, feather, secure
Climb, configuration, control, checklist
why: Control comes first, using aileron and rudder aggressively if needed. Then the memory items configure the airplane for climb, then the bank is reduced to the best-climb angle, and last come the printed checklist and the securing checklist.

q: In the 'Climb' step after an engine failure, once control and configuration are set, how should the bank angle be adjusted?
a: Reduced to the angle that gives the best climb performance
d: Increased to 10–15° toward the operating engine for more control
Rolled to wings level with the ball centered
Banked a few degrees toward the dead engine to reduce drag
why: A steeper bank helps the rudder at first. Once the airplane is under control, you shallow it to the zero-sideslip bank, which gives the best climb. The Seneca POH 3-11 simply calls for 5° of bank toward the operating engine.
drop_reason: duplicate of o6-085 and o7-045 (after control is established, reduce bank to the zero-sideslip/best-climb angle)

q: Shortly after liftoff an engine fails, and even with full power on the other you can't climb. What speed gives the slowest sink rate?
a: Vyse
d: Vxse
Vsse
Vmc
why: Vyse is the best single-engine rate-of-climb speed, so when a climb isn't possible it gives the least rate of sink (drift-down).

q: After an engine failure on departure, what two bank angles are used, in order?
a: First a bank for directional control, then a zero-sideslip bank for climb
d: First a zero-sideslip bank for control, then a steeper bank for best climb
First wings level for control, then a bank toward the dead engine for climb
First a bank toward the dead engine, then wings level for climb
why: The first bank toward the good engine helps the rudder overcome the yaw from asymmetric thrust. Once you have control, you move to the shallower zero-sideslip bank, a technique for coordinated flight and best climb rather than a fixed number.

q: In a typical light twin, per the OEG, what bank helps the rudder right after an engine failure, while you pitch for Vyse?
a: 5 to 10 degrees toward the operating engine
d: 2 to 3 degrees toward the operating engine
15 to 20 degrees toward the operating engine
5 to 10 degrees toward the inoperative engine
why: Per the OEG, 5–10° toward the good engine helps the rudder at first; the smaller zero-sideslip bank (about 2°: 2–3° in the exam tip, 1.5–2.5° in OEG 3B-12) follows for best climb. Never bank toward the dead engine. The Seneca POH 3-11 says to maintain 5° of bank toward the operating engine.

q: In a typical light twin, per the OEG, what bank and ball position give zero sideslip for best climb at Vyse?
a: About 2–3° bank, ball slightly toward the operating engine
d: About 5–10° bank toward the operating engine, ball centered
Wings level, ball centered
About 2–3° bank, ball slightly toward the inoperative engine
why: A small bank toward the good engine, with the ball slightly toward that side, cancels the sideslip and minimizes drag; wings level with the ball centered leaves a sideslip. 2–3° is the OEG exam tip's figure; OEG 3B-12 gives 1.5–2.5°, so think 'about 2°'. The Seneca POH 3-11 instead calls for 5° of bank toward the operating engine.

q: Per the ACS, what minimum altitude must be reached before an evaluator may simulate an engine failure after liftoff?
a: 400 feet AGL
d: 200 feet AGL
500 feet AGL
1,000 feet AGL
why: The ACS sets 400 feet AGL as the minimum, along with at least Vsse, Vxse or Vyse. The OEG recommends the same limits for practice.
src: OEG 3C-26 · Private ACS PA.IX.F (App 2) · Commercial ACS CA.IX.F (App 2) · FAA-P-8740-66

q: Besides altitude, what airspeed must be reached before an engine failure is simulated after liftoff?
a: At least Vsse, Vxse, or Vyse
d: At least Vmc
At least rotation speed (Vr)
At least 1.1 times Vso
why: The evaluator may not simulate a failure until the airplane is at least 400 feet AGL and at least at the safe single-engine speed (Vsse), Vxse or Vyse. Vmc or rotation speed leaves no margin.
src: OEG 3C-26 · Private ACS PA.IX.F (App 2) · Commercial ACS CA.IX.F (App 2) · FAA-P-8740-66

q: Right after takeoff, why does the OEG value altitude over airspeed in excess of Vyse?
a: Extra speed can't easily be converted to needed altitude or distance
d: Extra speed raises Vmc and so reduces your margin of directional control
Extra speed overheats both engines during the initial climb
Extra speed keeps the failed propeller from feathering fully
why: Once at a safe height a twin can hold level on one engine far more easily than it can climb, and spare altitude can be cashed in for speed or glide distance. Spare airspeed can't be turned into the height you need nearly as readily.

q: An engine fails just after gear retraction, near the single-engine ceiling, with no runway left. What should you do with the gear?
a: Leave it up until committed to a landing; extending it costs climb
d: Lower it immediately; a twin should never be landed with the gear up
Lower it to stabilize the airplane, then try to climb
Cycle it down and up again to confirm the hydraulic system still works
why: Lowering the gear can cost the climb you badly need, so wait until you are positioned to land. Controlled off-airport engine-out landings, even gear up, usually turn out well. The Seneca POH 3-13 likewise says not to extend the gear until certain of making the field.

q: Compared with a failure at low altitude, what does an engine failure in cruise give you, and what stays the same?
a: Time to diagnose and fix it; control is still the top priority
d: Time to diagnose it; you never need to feather an engine in cruise
Better control; calling ATC now comes before flying
No extra time; you must still feather at once, just as down low
why: Cruise speed improves control and altitude buys time, so diagnosis and a fix may be possible. Flying the airplane still comes first.

q: If an en route engine failure can't be corrected, what does the OEG recommend?
a: Do the manufacturer's single-engine procedure; land as soon as possible
d: Continue on to the planned destination as long as fuel permits
Keep attempting restarts until the failed engine is running normally again
Climb to the single-engine service ceiling and hold there
why: If you can't fix the problem, run the manufacturer's single-engine procedure and get on the ground as soon as possible. Repeated restarts and pressing on to the destination add risk.

q: Once the immediate emergency is handled, what is the main problem after an en route engine failure?
a: Keeping enough altitude to reach the nearest suitable airport
d: Keeping the failed engine warm enough for a later restart attempt
Maintaining the planned cruise airspeed and ETA to the destination
Keeping fuel balanced between the two tanks
why: Whether you can hold enough altitude to reach a suitable airport depends on density altitude, gross weight, and the elevation of terrain and obstructions.

q: An engine fails at 11,000 ft, above the airplane's single-engine absolute ceiling. What will happen, and what speed should you fly?
a: It slowly loses altitude; fly Vyse to minimize the descent
d: It holds altitude; fly Vyse to maintain it
It slowly loses altitude; fly Vxse to minimize the descent
It holds altitude; fly Vmc to minimize drag
why: Above the single-engine absolute ceiling the airplane can't hold altitude and slowly drifts down. Vyse keeps the rate of altitude loss as low as possible.

q: Per the OEG, many en route power losses come from what cause, with what simple fix?
a: Fuel starvation; select another fuel tank
d: Magneto failure; switch both magnetos off
Induction icing; lean the mixture fully
Oil starvation; reduce the power to idle
why: Fuel starvation is a common cause, and switching tanks often brings the power back; in the Seneca, the POH 3-11 restore-power note includes crossfeed. A methodical check of gauges and switches, alternate air or carb heat, single magnetos, mixture and boost pump also helps.

q: En route, one engine's fuel flow and pressure begin to fluctuate and you suspect fuel vapor. What does the OEG suggest?
a: Turn on that engine's electric fuel boost pump
d: Pull that engine's mixture to cutoff briefly
Close that engine's cowl flap to warm it up
Turn that engine's magnetos off and back on
why: When vapor is suspected, running the boost pump can clear the fuel flow and pressure fluctuations. An engine that runs rough may also run smoothly on one magneto or at lower power.

q: A turbocharged engine loses power at high altitude and you suspect the turbocharger has failed. What might restore some power?
a: Lean the mixture further and/or descend to a lower altitude
d: Enrich the mixture fully and climb to a higher altitude
Close the throttle partway and select alternate air
Increase propeller RPM and climb to a higher altitude
why: Without boost, the engine gets too much fuel for the thin air, so leaning helps. At a lower altitude it runs better as what is now a normally aspirated engine.

q: After feathering a failed engine, which actions normally complete securing it?
a: Fuel (mixture, pump, selector), ignition and alternator off; cowl flap closed
d: Fuel on (pump, selector); ignition and alternator off; cowl flap open
Fuel (mixture, pump, selector) and ignition off; alternator on; cowl flap open
Fuel and ignition left on for a restart; alternator off; cowl flap closed
why: Securing cuts off fuel, spark and electrical load to the dead engine, and closing its cowl flap reduces drag. Pressurized twins may also have a bleed-air valve to close. The Seneca POH 3-11 feathering procedure covers the same items.

q: An engine was shut down in flight because of an oil leak. Why is an attempted restart risky?
a: More engine damage, a worse leak, or an in-flight fire
d: The propeller will automatically re-feather on restart
The starter will not engage when oil pressure is low
The restart will discharge the battery below minimums
why: An engine shut down for a mechanical reason can be damaged further if it's restarted, and an oil or fuel leak can get worse and start a fire. Leave it secured unless there is a compelling reason.

q: During a restart attempt, the prop comes out of feather but the engine won't start, and the prop can't be re-feathered. Why?
a: Windmilling RPM is too low, so the start locks block feathering
d: The unfeathering accumulator must be recharged before feathering
The prop governor stays locked at its high-RPM stop after unfeathering
The feathering spring is damaged by every unfeathering cycle
why: If the prop windmills below the start-lock disengagement speed, the locks stay engaged and it can't return to feather; the windmilling drag may make level flight impossible. The Seneca can be feathered only above 800 RPM (POH 3-11).

q: What is the result if the propeller is left windmilling after a failed in-flight restart?
a: Significant drag; the airplane may be unable to hold level flight
d: Less drag than a feathered prop, so climb performance improves
About the same drag as a feathered prop, so nothing changes
Only a small loss of cruise speed, with no effect on climb
why: A windmilling prop produces far more drag than a feathered one, which can turn a manageable single-engine cruise into a forced descent.

q: Citing SAIB CE-05-51, what risk does the OEG warn of when shutting down and restarting an engine for training?
a: A faulty restart may leave a dead engine: a real emergency
d: Feathering at altitude may damage the propeller governor
A restart using the starter may overheat the battery
A feathered prop may unfeather itself during the descent
why: A practice shutdown can turn into an actual engine-out emergency if the restart goes wrong. Always follow the manufacturer's restart checklist and weigh all the hazards before shutting down for training.

q: Per the OEG, how should a typical light twin's single-engine traffic pattern compare with a normal two-engine pattern?
a: Essentially the same altitudes, airspeeds, and key positions
d: Lower and tighter, to minimize the time spent flying on one engine
A long, flat, low final to stay close to the runway
Flown at Vxse throughout for a steeper descent
why: The OEG treats an OEI pattern as basically a normal one: similar altitudes, speeds and key points, and no long, flat, low final. The Seneca POH 3-13 adds: carry extra altitude and speed on the approach.

q: Per the OEG, in a typical light twin with adequate performance, when should the gear be confirmed down on a single-engine approach?
a: No later than abeam the intended point of landing
d: No later than the start of the turn onto the base leg
No later than 500 feet AGL on the final approach
Only once over the runway threshold
why: Per the OEG, with adequate performance the gear can go down on downwind and should be confirmed down by the abeam point. The Seneca POH 3-13 differs: don't extend the gear until certain of making the field.

q: Per the OEG, what is the minimum airspeed on a single-engine approach until the landing is assured?
a: Vyse
d: Vxse
Vmc
1.3 Vso
why: Hold at least Vyse on downwind, base and final, because it keeps the best performance available until the landing is certain; slow to 1.3 Vso or the POH speed only after that. The Seneca POH 3-13 final approach speed is 105 mph, its Vyse.

q: On base with one engine out, your airspeed is decaying and the sink rate is high. What does the OEG say about more flaps?
a: Delay further flap extension until closer to the runway
d: Extend full flaps now to steepen the approach
Extend flaps and slow below Vyse to cut the sink
Retract all flaps and climb back to pattern altitude
why: Decaying airspeed or a high sink rate means performance is inadequate, so hold off on more flaps until closer to the runway; Vyse stays the minimum. The Seneca POH 3-13 says no flaps until certain of making the field, and 25° rather than full.

q: In a typical light twin, per the OEG, once a single-engine landing is assured, to what speed do you slow?
a: 1.3 Vso, or the POH/AFM recommended speed
d: Vmc, to minimize the total landing distance
Vxse, to steepen the final descent angle
Vsse, to keep a safety margin
why: Hold Vyse until the landing is assured, then slow to 1.3 Vso or the speed the POH/AFM recommends; final flaps can wait, or you can land with partial flaps. The Seneca POH 3-13 gives 105 mph for the single-engine final approach.

q: Which approach profile should be avoided on a single-engine final?
a: A long, flat, low approach
d: A normal 3° glidepath
A slightly steeper than normal approach
Following the VASI glidepath
why: A normal 3° path is preferred, ideally using a VASI or similar aid, and slightly steeper is acceptable. A long, flat, low approach needs more power and leaves no margin if you come up short.

q: Besides a long, flat approach, what does the OEG say to avoid on a single-engine final?
a: Large, sudden power applications or reductions
d: Landing with only partial flaps, rather than full flaps
Using a VASI or other visual glidepath aid
Delaying the final flap setting
why: Big, abrupt power changes on one engine cause big yaw changes and make control harder. Landing with partial flaps, delaying final flaps and using a VASI are all acceptable.

q: Per the OEG, when should a typical light twin be configured and stabilized for a single-engine instrument approach?
a: Before reaching the final approach fix
d: At the decision altitude or MDA
Just after crossing the final approach fix
At the missed approach point
why: Configuring before the FAF (or on downwind for a VFR pattern) lets you stabilize, reduces Vmc effects and frees your attention for flying. The Seneca POH 3-13 is more conservative: no gear or flaps until certain of making the field.

q: Per the OEG, are single-engine go-arounds recommended in a light twin?
a: No; on final with gear and flaps down, you're committed to land
d: Yes; they are safer than landing long on a single engine
Yes, as long as the airspeed stays above Vmc throughout
No; Part 23 prohibits go-arounds with an engine inoperative
why: A light twin generally can't climb on one engine with gear and flaps down, and cleaning up while holding Vyse costs a lot of altitude. The Seneca POH 3-13 also says to avoid one if at all possible and gives a procedure only for when it can't be avoided.

q: On short final with one engine out, gear and flaps down, a vehicle enters the runway. Per the OEG, what is the best choice?
a: Land on another runway, a taxiway, or the grass
d: Go around at full power on the operating engine
Retract the flaps and climb away at Vxse
Slow to Vmc and extend the final approach
why: Once configured on final with one engine, you are committed to land. If the intended runway is blocked, land on another runway, a taxiway or the infield rather than attempt a single-engine go-around.

q: Roughly how much altitude can a light twin lose while retracting gear and flaps at Vyse in a single-engine go-around?
a: 500 feet or more
d: About 50 feet
About 100 feet
None, if Vyse is held
why: Losses of 500 feet or more are not unusual. If the gear went down by an alternate (emergency) method, it may not retract at all, which wipes out nearly all climb ability.

q: You start a go-around from short final with the gear down and full flaps. Unless the POH says otherwise, what do you retract first?
a: The flaps (at least partially), then the gear
d: The gear first, then the flaps
Gear and flaps together, immediately
The gear first; flaps after 1,000 feet AGL
why: After setting climb attitude and power, bring the flaps up partially or to the takeoff setting. Retract the gear once a positive rate of climb is established and you are sure the airplane will stay airborne. Your school's Seneca go-around does the same: flaps to 25°, gear up on a positive rate, then the rest of the flaps.

q: Why are the flaps generally retracted before the gear during a go-around?
a: Full flaps add more drag than gear, and gear down helps if you touch down
d: The gear adds more drag than full flaps do, and the flaps improve the climb
The gear motor cannot run while the flaps are still moving
Retracting the gear first makes the airplane pitch down sharply near the ground
why: On most airplanes full flaps cause more drag than the gear. Leaving the gear down and locked also protects you if the airplane touches down as the go-around begins.

q: Why should flaps be retracted in small increments during a go-around?
a: A sudden full retraction loses lift and can settle the airplane
d: The flap motor overheats if it is run continuously for long
Small increments keep the airspeed safely below Vfe
Small increments keep the gear warning horn from sounding
why: Raising the flaps a little at a time lets the airplane accelerate as lift is reduced. Dumping them all at once can make it sink back toward the ground.

q: In a very low go-around, the airplane settles onto the runway and bounces. How does the OEG view this?
a: Not a big danger if kept straight at a steady, safe pitch
d: An emergency that calls for an immediate power reduction
A cue to retract the landing gear at once to reduce drag
A cue to pull the nose up sharply and climb away quickly
why: Go-around power brings the airplane to flying speed quickly and softens any second contact with the runway. Keep it straight, hold the pitch, and raise the gear only once you are sure it will stay airborne.

q: Per the OEG, if a second pilot is aboard, what should you agree on before takeoff to reduce engine-failure risk?
a: Pilot flying and pilot not flying duties in an emergency
d: Which pilot will do the cruise fuel and power planning
That both pilots share the controls during any emergency
That the second pilot stays hands-off and silent throughout
why: Settling in advance who flies and who handles checklists, radios and callouts prevents both pilots grabbing the controls, or neither acting, when an engine quits.
